explanation.body: At the top, tension and weight both act inward, so $1.2+0.040(9.81)=mv^2/0.30$ and $\tfrac12mv^2=0.23886\ \mathrm{J}$. By conservation of energy, $0.23886+0.040(9.81)(2\times0.30)=\tfrac12(0.040)u^2$, giving $u^2=23.715\ \mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$ at the bottom. The centripetal acceleration there is $u^2/r=23.715/0.30=79.1\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

perOption.A: Uses the centripetal acceleration at the top.
perOption.B: Uses one radius for the vertical drop between the top and bottom.
perOption.C: Omits the ball’s weight when finding its speed at the top.
perOption.D: Correct. The ball gains kinetic energy over a drop of two radii.

difficultyReason: The student must find the speed at the top from the radial forces and then use energy conservation to find the speed at the bottom.
misconception: Using the same speed at the top and bottom.
transcription:
A small ball of mass $0.040\ \mathrm{kg}$ is attached to a light string and rotates in a vertical circle of radius $0.30\ \mathrm{m}$. When the ball is vertically above the centre of the circle, the tension in the string is $1.2\ \mathrm{N}$.

[The ball is at the top of a dashed circle, with the string running vertically down to the centre. The radius is labelled $0.30\ \mathrm{m}$.]

What is the centripetal acceleration of the ball when it is vertically below the centre of the circle?

A $40\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$
B $59\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$
C $69\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$
D $79\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$

explanation.body: On S to Q, $G_1$ has a nonzero minimum, indicating that the stars have different masses. On P to R, $G_3$ starts at a lower field strength than it ends, indicating that X is less massive than Y. The zero-field point lies closer to X, so the spacecraft can spend about as long covering the shorter distance from P to that point at lower speeds as it spends covering the longer distance to R at higher speeds.

perOption.A: With unequal masses, the symmetric endpoints P and R have different field magnitudes.
perOption.B: Correct. The perpendicular path has no cancellation, and the axial path crosses a zero closer to X.
perOption.C: A zero on S to Q would require equal masses, which also give a zero between P and R.
perOption.D: A zero on S to Q would imply equal masses, which give equal field magnitudes at P and R.

issues: B is the intended qualitative match. A zero between P and R requires a suitable mass ratio, which is unspecified. At a zero crossed with nonzero speed, the magnitude should have a cusp, whereas the printed graph shows a smooth minimum.
difficultyReason: The student must compare vector cancellation along two paths and account for the effect of acceleration on the time axis.
misconception: Assuming equidistant points always have zero resultant field.
transcription:
The diagram shows two stars, X and Y and 5 points, O, P, Q, R and S.
O is the midpoint of the line joining the centres of X and Y.
P and R are on the line joining the centres of X and Y and are at the same distance from the centres of X and Y respectively.
Q and S are on the perpendicular bisector of the line joining P and R and are at the same distance from O.

[X, P, O, R and Y lie left to right along a dashed horizontal line. Q is above O and S is below O on a dashed perpendicular line.]

A spacecraft travels with constant acceleration in its direction of travel between 2 points.

Graphs $G_1$, $G_2$ and $G_3$ show the possible variations in the magnitude of the resultant gravitational field strength $g$ due to the stars at the position of the spacecraft with time $t$.

[All three graphs plot $g$ vertically and $t$ horizontally. $G_1$ falls to a positive minimum after halfway and rises to its starting value. $G_2$ falls to zero after halfway and rises to its starting value. $G_3$ falls to zero near halfway and rises to a value above its starting value.]

Which graphs correspond to the motions of the spacecraft from S to Q and P to R?

Option | S to Q | P to R
A | $G_1$ | $G_2$
B | $G_1$ | $G_3$
C | $G_2$ | $G_1$
D | $G_2$ | $G_3$

explanation.body: The potential at Q is $\phi_Q=-2.0\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$. Since potential is inversely proportional to distance from P, $\phi_R/\phi_Q=PQ/PR=1/4$, so $\phi_R=-0.5\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$. The external work is $m(\phi_R-\phi_Q)=3.0(-0.5+2.0)=4.5\ \mathrm{J}$. The external force points in the direction of the displacement from Q to R, so its work is positive.

perOption.A: Multiplies the potential at Q by the distance ratio $QR/PQ=3$ and treats that value as the potential change.
perOption.B: Reverses the potential difference by subtracting the final potential from the initial potential.
perOption.C: Correct. The gravitational potential increases from Q to R.
perOption.D: Treats the distance ratio as a multiplier for the potential change instead of calculating the two potentials.

issues: The key prints J for the potential at R. The explanation uses J/kg.
difficultyReason: The student must work out the distance ratio from the sphere’s centre and then use the signed difference in potential.
misconception: Using QR as the distance of R from the sphere’s centre.
transcription:
Point P is at the centre of a uniform sphere M. The work done by an external force in bringing a mass of $1.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ from infinity to point Q is $-2.0\ \mathrm{J}$.

[Sphere M is shown in cross-section with P at its centre. A dashed horizontal line runs right from P through Q to R, both outside the sphere.]

The ratio $\frac{PQ}{QR}$ is $\frac{1}{3}$.

What is the work done by an external force to bring a mass of $3.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ from Q to R?

A $-18\ \mathrm{J}$
B $-4.5\ \mathrm{J}$
C $4.5\ \mathrm{J}$
D $18\ \mathrm{J}$

explanation.body: In simple harmonic motion, $a=-\omega^2x$, so acceleration and displacement have opposite signs whenever they are nonzero. The two curves have coincident zeros and opposite signs, so P can be acceleration and Q displacement.

perOption.A: Correct. Acceleration and displacement are half a period out of phase.
perOption.B: Acceleration and velocity are a quarter period apart.
perOption.C: Displacement and velocity are a quarter period apart.
perOption.D: The oscillatory potential energy is proportional to displacement squared and varies at twice the frequency of velocity.

difficultyReason: The opposite signs and simultaneous zero crossings identify the acceleration–displacement pair.
misconception: Confusing a quarter-period phase difference with a half-period phase difference.
transcription:
The two graphs below are for the motion of a body undergoing simple harmonic motion.

[Two graphs have time on their horizontal axes and P and Q on their respective vertical axes. Both curves start at zero and are sinusoidal with the same period. P initially rises, Q initially falls, and their zero crossings coincide.]

What could be represented by the quantities P and Q?

Option | P | Q
A | acceleration | displacement
B | acceleration | velocity
C | displacement | velocity
D | potential energy | velocity

explanation.body: The total energy equals the maximum kinetic energy, $E=\tfrac12mv_0^2=\tfrac12m(\omega x_0)^2=2\pi^2mx_0^2/T^2$. With $x'_0=2x_0$ and $T'=3T$, $E'=(x'_0/x_0)^2(T/T')^2E=2^2(1/3)^2(18)=8.0\ \mathrm{mJ}$.

perOption.A: Divides by four for the amplitude change instead of multiplying by four.
perOption.B: Correct. The energy is multiplied by four and divided by nine.
perOption.C: Accounts for the amplitude change but ignores the longer period.
perOption.D: Multiplies by nine for the longer period instead of dividing by nine.

difficultyReason: The student must combine two squared scale factors with opposite effects on the energy.
misconception: Treating total energy as proportional to the square of the period.

explanation.body: By Malus’ law, $I_1/I_0=\cos^2 20^\circ$ and $I_2/I_1=\cos^2(\theta-20^\circ)$. Multiplying gives $I_2/I_0=\cos^2 20^\circ\cos^2(\theta-20^\circ)=0.25$. Taking the positive square root gives $\cos(\theta-20^\circ)=0.50/\cos 20^\circ=0.53209$. Hence $\theta-20^\circ=57.853^\circ$ and $\theta=77.853^\circ\approx78^\circ$.

perOption.A: Subtracts the first filter’s angle from the angle between the axes instead of adding it.
perOption.B: Reports the angle between the two transmission axes as the angle from vertical.
perOption.C: Correct. The second transmission axis is about $78^circ$ from vertical.
perOption.D: Treats the intensity ratio as a cosine instead of a squared cosine.

difficultyReason: Applying Malus’ law twice requires tracking the new polarisation direction after the first filter.
misconception: Measuring both Malus’ law angles from the incident polarisation.
transcription:
A beam of vertically polarised light of intensity $I_0$ is transmitted through two polarising filters $\mathrm{P}_1$ and $\mathrm{P}_2$ as shown. The axes of polarisation of $\mathrm{P}_1$ and $\mathrm{P}_2$ are $20^\circ$ and $\theta$ relative to the direction of polarisation of the incident light. The intensity of the light after passing through $\mathrm{P}_2$ is $0.25 I_0$.

[Vertically plane polarised light of intensity $I_0$ travels from left to right through $\mathrm{P}_1$ and then $\mathrm{P}_2$. Their transmission axes tilt to the same side of the vertical by $20^\circ$ and $\theta$, respectively.]

What is the value of $\theta$?

A $38^\circ$
B $58^\circ$
C $78^\circ$
D $95^\circ$

explanation.body: The string forms a stationary wave, and E and F lie in adjacent loops, so their phase difference is $\pi$. Both particles have the same period, but F has a larger amplitude, giving it a greater maximum speed and hence a greater maximum kinetic energy.

perOption.A: Uses the progressive-wave phase formula and assumes equal maximum kinetic energies despite different amplitudes.
perOption.B: Uses the progressive-wave phase formula for points in adjacent stationary-wave loops.
perOption.C: Assumes equal maximum kinetic energies despite F’s larger amplitude.
perOption.D: Correct. Adjacent loops oscillate in antiphase and F has the greater maximum kinetic energy.

difficultyReason: The student must read both the loop positions and the relative amplitudes from the stationary-wave diagram.
misconception: Applying progressive-wave phase differences to a stationary wave.
transcription:
A string of length $L$ is stretched between two fixed points G and H and made to vibrate transversely as shown below.

[Solid and dashed curves show opposite extremes of a three-loop stationary wave between G on the left and H on the right. E is in the middle loop near its left node, and F is at the antinode of the right-hand loop. The horizontal distance from E to F is labelled $s$ and the distance from G to H is labelled $L$.]

Two particles E and F on the string are separated by a distance $s$. The maximum kinetic energies of particles E and F are $K_{\mathrm{E}}$ and $K_{\mathrm{F}}$ respectively.

Which of the following gives the correct phase difference and relationship between maximum kinetic energies of the particles?

Option | phase difference / rad | maximum kinetic energy
A | $\frac{3s}{2L}\times2\pi$ | same
B | $\frac{3s}{2L}\times2\pi$ | $K_{\mathrm{E}}<K_{\mathrm{F}}$
C | $\pi$ | same
D | $\pi$ | $K_{\mathrm{E}}<K_{\mathrm{F}}$

explanation.body: For the first order, use $d\sin\theta=\lambda$ with $d=1/(5.0\times10^5)\ \mathrm{m}$. Substituting $700\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{m}$ for red gives $\theta_{\mathrm{red}}=20.49^\circ$, and substituting $400\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{m}$ for blue gives $\theta_{\mathrm{blue}}=11.54^\circ$. The angular separation is $20.49^\circ-11.54^\circ=8.95^\circ\approx9.0^\circ$.

perOption.A: Correct. The angular separation is the difference between the two first-order angles.
perOption.B: Gives only the blue diffraction angle from the grating normal.
perOption.C: Gives only the red diffraction angle from the grating normal.
perOption.D: Adds the first-order angles as if the two rays were on opposite sides of the normal.

difficultyReason: The student must calculate two first-order diffraction angles and subtract them.
misconception: Adding angles measured on the same side of the grating normal.
transcription:
White light covers the range of wavelength from $400\ \mathrm{nm}$ to $700\ \mathrm{nm}$. A diffraction grating with $5.0\times10^5$ lines per metre is placed perpendicular to a ray of white light and produces the first order spectrum as shown.

[White light travels horizontally from the left through a vertical grating. To the right, a ray continues straight and the blue and red first-order rays diverge above it, with red above blue. The angle $\theta$ is marked between the red and blue rays.]

What is the angle $\theta$ between the red and blue ends of the spectrum?

A $9.0^\circ$
B $12^\circ$
C $20^\circ$
D $32^\circ$

explanation.body: From $pV=nRT$, constant-pressure compression lowers $T$, so it is a horizontal segment directed left on the $p$–$T$ graph. During constant-temperature expansion, $p$ falls, giving a downward vertical segment. At constant volume, $p\propto T$, so the upward-sloping segment lies on a straight line through the origin.

perOption.A: Correct. All three segments match the gas processes and their directions.
perOption.B: Shows temperature rising during constant-pressure compression and curves the constant-volume segment.
perOption.C: Shows temperature changing during the constant-temperature expansion.
perOption.D: The constant-volume line does not pass through the origin when extended.

difficultyReason: The student must translate each leg of a cycle into new coordinates and distinguish proportionality from a merely linear relation.
misconception: Assuming the shape of a process is unchanged when the horizontal variable changes.

explanation.body: The coil’s temperature is constant, so $\Delta U=0$. Electrical work is done on the coil at $500\ \mathrm{W}$, and the coil continues to lose heat to the water. The first law therefore gives $\mathrm{d}Q/\mathrm{d}t=-500\ \mathrm{W}$ for heat supplied to the coil.

perOption.A: Treats electrical work as heat entering the coil and assumes its internal energy continues to rise.
perOption.B: Ignores heat leaving the coil at steady temperature.
perOption.C: Reverses the signs of the outgoing heat transfer and the incoming electrical work.
perOption.D: Correct. Heat leaves at the same rate that electrical work is done on the coil.

difficultyReason: The student must identify electrical work as the input and apply the first law at constant temperature.
misconception: Classifying the electrical energy entering the coil as heat.
transcription:
A $500\ \mathrm{W}$ electric kettle is used to boil water and is left on even after the water begins to boil. After 5 minutes, the temperature of its heating coil reaches a constant value.

When the first law of thermodynamics is used to quantitatively describe the heating coil after this time, which row correctly describes the application of the first law?

Option | rate of increase of internal energy / W | rate of heat supplied to the coil / W | rate of work done on the coil / W
A | $+500$ | $+500$ | $0$
B | $+500$ | $0$ | $+500$
C | $0$ | $+500$ | $-500$
D | $0$ | $-500$ | $+500$

explanation.body: Take right as positive. The electron is attracted towards $+Q$ at X and repelled away from $-Q$ at Y, so both forces point left throughout the interval. The key’s resultant-force curve stays negative and is closest to zero at the midpoint, where the force magnitude is smallest.

perOption.A: Correct. The force points left and is weakest at the midpoint.
perOption.B: Uses the direction of the electric field as the force direction for a negative charge.
perOption.C: Treats the midpoint as a maximum even though each inverse-square force grows sharply near its source.
perOption.D: Reverses the force direction for an electron and places the magnitude maximum at the midpoint.

difficultyReason: The student must combine attraction and repulsion and determine where their combined inverse-square magnitude is smallest.
misconception: Using the electric field direction as the force direction on an electron.
transcription:
A point charge of $+Q$ is placed at X and a point charge of $-Q$ is placed at Y.

[X is on the left and Y is on the right, joined by a dashed horizontal line. The charges $+Q$ and $-Q$ are marked at X and Y respectively.]

What happens to the electric force acting on an electron as it moves in a straight line from X to Y?

Option | magnitude of force | direction of force
A | decreases to a minimum at midpoint of XY and increases | always towards the left
B | decreases to a minimum at midpoint of XY and increases | always towards the right
C | increases to a maximum at midpoint of XY and decreases | always towards the left
D | increases to a maximum at midpoint of XY and decreases | always towards the right

explanation.body: The stationary drop initially has its weight balanced by the electric force, so $mg=|q|(5000/d)$. At the new voltage the upward electric force is $|q|(4000/d)=\tfrac45mg=0.8mg$. Taking downwards as positive, $mg-0.8mg=ma$, so $a=1.96\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, or $2.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ downwards.

perOption.A: Reports the fraction $0.20$ of $g$ as the acceleration without multiplying by $g$.
perOption.B: Correct. The net downward force is $0.20mg$.
perOption.C: Uses the acceleration due to the new electric force alone, ignoring weight.
perOption.D: Adds the electric force and weight even though they act in opposite directions.

difficultyReason: The student must use the initial balance to express the reduced electric force as a fraction of the drop’s weight.
misconception: Using the reduced electric force as the net force.
transcription:
An oil drop, carrying a charge of $-3.2\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, is stationary in the region between two horizontal plates when the potential difference between the two plates is $5.0\times10^3\ \mathrm{V}$. The separation of the plates is $16\ \mathrm{mm}$.

What is the initial acceleration of the oil drop when the potential difference is decreased to $4.0\times10^3\ \mathrm{V}$?

A $0.20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$
B $2.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$
C $7.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$
D $18\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$

explanation.body: The current through the specimen is the same at every section, so $I_X=I_Y=I_Z$. Since $I=nevA$ and $I$, $n$ and $e$ are constant, drift speed varies inversely with cross-sectional area. X is narrowest and Y widest, giving $v_X>v_Z>v_Y$.

perOption.A: Assumes constant current implies constant drift speed despite the changing area.
perOption.B: Correct. The same current passes through all three sections, with faster drift in narrower sections.
perOption.C: Assigns different currents to sections of an unbranched conductor and overlooks the inverse dependence of drift speed on area.
perOption.D: Allows the steady current to decrease between X and the other sections without a branch.

issues: The printed opening line of the question is a sentence fragment, preserved in the transcription.
difficultyReason: The student must distinguish conservation of current from variation in drift speed with area.
misconception: Assuming current decreases where a conductor widens.
transcription:
An electric current $I$ in a flat metal specimen of uniform thickness and of the shape shown.

[The specimen is narrow at section X, widens to its maximum at Y, then tapers through the intermediate-width section Z before becoming narrow again. The arrow for $I$ points right.]

Which of the following correctly describes the magnitude of the current $I$ and drift velocity $v$ at sections X, Y and Z?

Option | $I$ | $v$
A | $I_X=I_Y=I_Z$ | $v_X=v_Y=v_Z$
B | $I_X=I_Y=I_Z$ | $v_X>v_Z>v_Y$
C | $I_X>I_Z>I_Y$ | $v_X=v_Y=v_Z$
D | $I_X>I_Z=I_Y$ | $v_X>v_Z>v_Y$

explanation.body: The $400\ \Omega$ and $600\ \Omega$ resistors are in parallel and have the same potential difference. Since $I=V/R$, the $600\ \Omega$ branch carries $\frac{400}{400+600}I=\frac25 I$. Using $P=I^2R$, the power ratio is $\frac{I^2(120)}{(\frac25 I)^2(600)}=1.25\approx1.3$.

perOption.A: Uses the same current in the $120\ \Omega$ resistor and the $600\ \Omega$ branch.
perOption.B: Uses the power dissipated by the entire parallel pair as the denominator.
perOption.C: Correct. The $600\ \Omega$ resistor carries two-fifths of the incoming current.
perOption.D: Assumes the $120\ \Omega$ and $600\ \Omega$ resistors have the same potential difference.

difficultyReason: The student must work out the current in the parallel branch before applying the squared-current power relation.
misconception: Using the total current for an individual parallel branch.
transcription:
Three resistors are arranged in a part of a circuit, and the resistance of each resistor is labelled as shown.

[Current $I$ flows to the right through a $120\ \Omega$ resistor, then divides into two parallel branches. The upper branch contains a $400\ \Omega$ resistor and the lower branch contains a $600\ \Omega$ resistor. The branches then rejoin.]

The current through the $120\ \Omega$ resistor is $I$.

What is the value of $\frac{\text{power dissipated in the }120\ \Omega\text{ resistor}}{\text{power dissipated in the }600\ \Omega\text{ resistor}}$?

A $0.20$
B $0.50$
C $1.3$
D $5.0$

explanation.body: The cells oppose each other, giving an effective e.m.f. of $5.0-3.0=2.0\ \mathrm{V}$. The potential difference across the $3.0\ \Omega$ resistor is $\frac{3.0}{2.0+3.0}(2.0)=1.2\ \mathrm{V}$. From X to Y via the right-hand side, the potential rises by $1.2\ \mathrm{V}$ across the resistor and by $3.0\ \mathrm{V}$ from the negative to the positive terminal of the cell, giving $4.2\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.A: Gives only the potential difference across the $2.0\ \Omega$ resistor.
perOption.B: Gives only the potential difference across the $3.0\ \Omega$ resistor.
perOption.C: Counts the rise across the $3.0$ V cell and omits the rise across the resistor.
perOption.D: Correct. The resistor and cell both contribute potential rises along the right-hand path from X to Y.

difficultyReason: The student must find the net e.m.f. and then track potential changes along a path between two circuit nodes.
misconception: Treating the p.d. across a single component as the p.d. between X and Y.
